title: Emergence of Homo sapiens in Africa
summary: Around 300,000 years ago our species, Homo sapiens, was taking shape in Africa. The oldest fossils of its lineage, from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, are dated to about 315,000 years ago and pair a modern-looking face with an older, elongated braincase.
card: Fossils, stone tools and genomes all place the origin of Homo sapiens in Africa during the Middle Pleistocene. Jebel Irhoud in Morocco (about 315,000 years ago), Florisbad in South Africa (about 259,000, disputed) and Omo Kibish in Ethiopia (at least 233,000) show the species' features appearing across the continent. Many researchers now think it arose from several linked populations rather than in one cradle.
what:
Homo sapiens, the species to which every living person belongs, evolved in Africa from earlier Middle Pleistocene humans, often grouped as Homo heidelbergensis or Homo rhodesiensis. Its emergence was a gradual process rather than a single event, and the fossil record of it is thin.

The oldest fossils now assigned to the H. sapiens lineage come from Jebel Irhoud, a karst cave in a limestone massif southeast of Safi, Morocco. Mining exposed the site in the early 1960s, and a nearly complete skull was found by accident. Excavations led by Jean-Jacques Hublin (Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology) and Abdelouahed Ben-Ncer (INSAP, Rabat) from 2004 raised the number of hominin fossils from 6 to 22, representing at least five individuals: three adults, an adolescent and a child of about eight. Thermoluminescence dating of burnt flint tools from the same layer gave a weighted average of 315,000 ± 34,000 years, and a re-dated tooth from the 1960s Irhoud 3 jaw gave 286,000 ± 32,000 years. Earlier estimates had put the fossils at about 40,000 and later 160,000 years, and had read them as an African Neanderthal or a late archaic group.

The Irhoud people had faces and teeth that fall within the range of living humans, but their braincases were long and low rather than globular. Their tools were Middle Stone Age Levallois flakes and points, and they hunted mainly gazelle.

Other early fossils lie far away. A partial skull from Florisbad, South Africa, has an ESR date of 259,000 ± 35,000 years on an associated tooth, although whether the tooth and skull belong together is disputed. Omo I from the Kibish Formation in southern Ethiopia, found in 1967 and long dated to about 195,000 years, is at least 233,000 ± 22,000 years old. Herto, also in Ethiopia, dates to about 160,000–155,000 years ago.

Researchers disagree on how to read this spread: some see a pan-African process among loosely connected populations, while others stress that Irhoud is only an early, partly archaic member of the lineage.

uncertainty.note: Start: thermoluminescence weighted average for Jebel Irhoud layer 7, 315 ± 34 ka at 1 sigma; the 95% range is 383–247 ka (Richter et al. 2017). End: the minimum age of Omo I, 233 ± 22 ka at 2 sigma (Vidal et al. 2022), chosen as the earliest dated fossil with fully modern cranial features; it is a minimum, and Hublin et al. argue braincase shape kept evolving within H. sapiens after this. Genetic estimates of the deepest population split range from 350–260 ka (Schlebusch et al. 2017) to 135–120 ka among present-day populations (Ragsdale et al. 2023), depending on the model. The process has no sharp start or end.

how: No single event made Homo sapiens. Three lines of evidence show how it happened. First, the fossils show a mosaic. At Jebel Irhoud the face, jaw and teeth were already within modern human variation by about 315,000 years ago, while the braincase stayed long and low. Hublin and colleagues infer that the face was established early and that later evolution mainly reshaped the brain and braincase, probably through genetic changes affecting brain organisation and development. Second, the tools. Levallois-based Middle Stone Age assemblages appear by about 300,000 years ago at Jebel Irhoud and Olorgesailie, before 275,000–285,000 years ago at Gademotta and in the Kapthurin Formation, and about 280,000 years ago at Florisbad. Richter and colleagues suggest the species and the technology emerged close together in time, possibly across the continent. Third, the environment and population structure. Middle Pleistocene green Sahara episodes, one especially marked around 330,000 years ago, shrank the desert and allowed ecological contact between north and sub-Saharan Africa. Scerri and colleagues argue that shifting habitats split early humans into subdivided populations linked by occasional gene flow, so modern traits appeared piecemeal in different places. Genetic models differ on the details: Schlebusch and colleagues put the deepest split among modern human populations at 350,000–260,000 years ago, while Ragsdale and colleagues model two or more weakly differentiated stem populations exchanging migrants, with the earliest divergence among living populations 120,000–135,000 years ago. Dating relies on thermoluminescence of burnt flint, ESR and U-series on teeth, and argon–argon dating of volcanic ash.
why_it_matters: Every person alive today belongs to the species whose beginnings these fossils record, and every later chapter of human history follows from it, from the dispersals out of Africa to the peopling of every continent. The 2017 Jebel Irhoud dates changed how that beginning is understood. Before them, most researchers placed a single cradle in East Africa about 200,000 years ago, based on Omo Kibish and Herto. The Moroccan fossils pushed the lineage back by roughly 100,000 years and put North Africa, long overlooked, at the centre of the debate. Together with Florisbad, the re-dating of Omo I to at least 233,000 years ago and new genetic models, this has shifted many researchers toward a picture of several linked African populations, with no single birthplace. That shift has a practical consequence for science: geneticists now test models with population structure and gene flow, and published split times now differ by more than 100,000 years depending on the model. Dating matters to the counterfactual too. Had Jebel Irhoud kept its earlier ages of about 40,000 or 160,000 years, its fossils would still be read as an African Neanderthal or a late archaic survivor, and the East African cradle model would face no North African challenge. Richter and colleagues also link the green Sahara episodes to continuity between the Maghreb and the rest of Africa. On that reasoning, without such humid windows the populations north and south of the desert would have been more isolated, and a continent-wide process would have been harder to sustain.

related.because: The African Homo sapiens populations that formed from about 300,000 years ago were the source of the much later dispersals that carried the species beyond Africa.

perspectives.holder: Hublin et al. (2017) and Richter et al. (2017), Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology and INSAP
perspectives.account: Jebel Irhoud, at about 315,000 years ago, documents an early stage of the H. sapiens clade, and with Florisbad shows the species' emergence involved the whole African continent, not sub-Saharan Africa alone. The Middle Stone Age arose at about the same time, and no single region should be favoured.

perspectives.holder: The earlier majority view, as described by the MPI-EVA press release and Richter et al. (2017)
perspectives.account: All living humans descend from one population in East Africa around 200,000 years ago, represented by the Omo Kibish (then dated to about 195,000 years) and Herto (about 160,000 years) fossils, the oldest with fully modern skulls.

perspectives.holder: Chris Stringer, Natural History Museum, London (2017)
perspectives.account: The Irhoud people are probable early members of the H. sapiens lineage with a mix of archaic and modern traits, not fully modern humans. Several early H. sapiens populations probably lived in different parts of Africa around 300,000 years ago, alongside other lineages such as H. naledi.

perspectives.holder: Scerri et al. (2018), 22 authors, Trends in Ecology & Evolution
perspectives.account: H. sapiens evolved within a set of subdivided, interlinked populations across Africa whose connections shifted with climate, so derived traits appeared in a mosaic. They call this African multiregionalism and reject a single panmictic origin.

perspectives.holder: Schlebusch et al. (2017), Science; Ragsdale et al. (2023), Nature
perspectives.account: Genomes give different split times depending on the model. Schlebusch's team places the deepest divergence among modern humans at 350,000–260,000 years ago. Ragsdale's team finds that two or more weakly differentiated stem populations linked by gene flow fit better than a single origin or archaic admixture, with present-day structure dating only to 120,000–135,000 years ago.

The 259,000-year ESR date comes from a tooth that may not belong with the Florisbad skull, and the spring deposits were disturbed, so current data do not show H. sapiens in southern Africa at about 260,000 years ago.

importance.justification: The origin of the species to which all living people belong is the starting point of all human history and a seed-list anchor, so it must be visible from whole-planet view.
